title: Levels of Cellular Organisation
subtitle: Unicellular, colonial and multicellular life
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: Compare the characteristics and structures of cells in unicellular, colonial and multicellular organisms
lessonIntent: Students can compare unicellular, colonial and multicellular organisation using cell specialisation, division of labour and interdependence rather than a universal survival-after-separation test.
examSkill: Compare the three levels on the same criteria: cell number, specialisation, division of labour and interdependence. Treat colonial-to-multicellular organisation as a spectrum in some lineages.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, how life goes from one cell doing everything to whole organisms. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: Why can a pond Amoeba live alone, but your liver cell can’t?
scenes.body: Every one of your cells came from one fertilised egg, yet a liver cell dies in pond water while a single-celled Amoeba thrives there.
scenes.callout: What did multicellular life trade away to become big?
scenes.caption: One cell that lives alone, colonies in between, and bodies of cells that can’t.

voiceover.text: Here's a puzzle. Every cell in your body came from one fertilised egg. But drop one of your liver cells into a glass of pond water, and it dies within hours. Drop in an Amoeba, which is just one cell, and it's perfectly happy. And somewhere in between sit colonies, like the green ball called Volvox, where lots of cells live together but stop just short of being one body. So what did multicellular life trade away to become big? Let's find out.

scenes.heading: One cell that does everything
scenes.body: A unicellular organism is a single cell that carries out every function of life on its own.

bullets.text: Examples: Amoeba, Paramecium, yeast and bacteria.
One cell handles nutrition, respiration, excretion, movement, sensitivity and reproduction.
So the cell is a generalist, carrying extra structures: pseudopodia, a contractile vacuole.

scenes.callout: One cell, every job: a structural generalist.
scenes.caption: An Amoeba moves and feeds with pseudopodia and pumps out water with a contractile vacuole.

verdict.text: One generalist cell performs every function of life

voiceover.text: Start at the simplest level. A unicellular organism is an organism whose whole body is one single cell, like an Amoeba, a Paramecium, yeast or bacteria. That one cell has to do every job of staying alive, nutrition, respiration, getting rid of waste, moving, sensing its surroundings and reproducing. So it's a generalist, and it carries structures a specialised cell would never need. An Amoeba pushes out pseudopodia to move and to engulf its food. And a contractile vacuole fills with the water that leaks in from the pond, then pumps it back out. One cell, every job.

scenes.heading: Colonial life: coordinated cells with limited specialisation
scenes.body: Colonial organisms contain multiple cells that remain relatively similar, with less division of labour than strongly multicellular organisms.

bullets.text: Gonium is a clear volvocine-colony example: a small sheet of similar flagellated cells that coordinate movement.
Colonial lineages can show intermediate levels of integration, so avoid a rigid 'independent cell versus body cell' rule.
Volvox is more specialised: species such as Volvox carteri have differentiated somatic and reproductive cells.

scenes.callout: Colonial and multicellular organisation can form a spectrum of integration.
scenes.caption: Colonies have multiple coordinated cells; some volvocine algae show intermediate specialisation.

verdict.text: Integration ranges from similar coordinated cells to specialised multicellularity

voiceover.text: Colonial life is best treated as a spectrum rather than a sharp survival test. A clear example is Gonium, a small colony of similar flagellated green-algal cells that coordinate their movement. Other volvocine algae show more integration. Volvox carteri, for example, has differentiated somatic cells and reproductive cells, so it should not be described as a ball of identical independent cells. The useful comparison is the degree of division of labour and interdependence.

scenes.heading: Multicellular: specialised and dependent
scenes.body: Multicellular organisms show sustained division of labour among specialised cell types that function as an integrated whole.

bullets.text: Specialised cell types perform different roles within tissues and organs.
Division of labour increases dependence among cell types, even though some cultured cells can survive outside the organism under suitable conditions.
Classify using specialisation, coordinated development and interdependence, not whether every isolated cell dies.

scenes.callout: Specialisation and division of labour are stronger evidence than a separation test.
scenes.caption: Multicellularity is characterised by specialised, interdependent cell types organised into a whole.

verdict.text: Specialisation and interdependence, not cell count

voiceover.text: Strong multicellularity is characterised by division of labour. Different cell types specialise for different jobs and work as an integrated organism. That creates interdependence, but do not turn that into the universal claim that every body cell dies as soon as it is separated; many animal and plant cells can survive in culture when supplied with suitable conditions. The stronger evidence is specialised cell types, coordinated development, tissues and sustained division of labour.

scenes.heading: The words you need
scenes.body: Five terms for comparing the three levels.

bullets.text: Unicellular: an organism whose entire body is one cell performing all life functions (Amoeba, yeast, bacteria).
Colonial: identical or near-identical cells living together, each largely able to survive alone (Volvox).
Multicellular: many specialised cells that depend on one another and cannot survive independently.
Cell specialisation: cells developing different structures suited to a particular function (differentiation).
Interdependence: cells relying on one another to survive, the hallmark of multicellular organisms.

scenes.caption: Unicellular, colonial, multicellular, cell specialisation, interdependence.

voiceover.text: Let's pin down the vocabulary. Unicellular means the entire organism is one cell that performs every life function, like an Amoeba, yeast or bacteria. Colonial means identical, or nearly identical, cells living together, where each cell could largely survive on its own, like Volvox. Multicellular means many specialised cells that depend on one another and can't survive independently. Cell specialisation, also called differentiation, is cells developing different structures suited to one particular job. And interdependence is cells relying on one another to survive, which is the hallmark of a multicellular organism.

scenes.heading: The liver cell and the Amoeba
scenes.question: A liver cell placed in pond water dies within hours, while an Amoeba in the same water thrives. Explain this difference by referring to the characteristics of cells at different levels of organisation.
scenes.coachNote: Explain means cause and effect. Name what any cell needs, then what each cell has or has lost.
steps: To survive alone a cell must obtain nutrients, exchange gases, remove wastes and control its water content.
The Amoeba is unicellular: a generalist with pseudopodia to feed and a contractile vacuole to expel water.
The liver cell is specialised: it lost those structures, and relies on the gut, lungs, blood and kidneys.
In pond water it takes in water by osmosis with no way to expel it, and gets no nutrients or oxygen.
Answer: specialisation buys efficiency at the price of independence, so the liver cell dies.
scenes.caption: The Amoeba keeps the structures for independent life; the specialised liver cell traded them away.

voiceover.text: Let's answer the hook as an exam question. Explain means cause and effect. First, name what any cell needs to survive alone. It has to get nutrients, exchange gases, remove wastes and control its water content. The Amoeba is unicellular, so it's a generalist. It feeds with pseudopodia, and its contractile vacuole pumps out the water that floods in from the pond. The liver cell is specialised. It lost those structures, and relies on the gut, the lungs, the blood and the kidneys to do those jobs for it. So in pond water, water rushes in by osmosis with no way out, and it gets no food or oxygen. Specialisation buys efficiency, but costs independence.

scenes.heading: A colony is just a multicellular organism?
scenes.body: Wrong: a colony and a multicellular organism are the same thing, both just many cells stuck together.
scenes.secondary: Right: colony cells are largely identical and each can survive alone; multicellular cells are specialised and interdependent, so a single cell can’t survive on its own.
scenes.mistakeTag: Cell count is not the test
scenes.callout: Ask: are the cells specialised, and could one live alone?
scenes.caption: The test is specialisation and interdependence, not the number of cells.

voiceover.text: Here's the trap. It's tempting to say a colony and a multicellular organism are the same thing, because both are just lots of cells stuck together. But the number of cells isn't the test. In a colony the cells are largely identical, and each one can survive on its own. In a multicellular organism the cells are specialised and interdependent, so a single cell can't survive alone. So whenever you're asked to classify an organism, ask two questions. Are the cells specialised? And could one of them live by itself?

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: Organism X is a small sheet of similar flagellated cells that coordinate movement but show little division of labour. Organism Y contains specialised nerve, muscle and digestive cells organised into tissues. Classify the organisation of each and justify.
scenes.pausePrompt: Pause: use specialisation and division of labour, not a survival-after-separation rule.
answerSteps: X is colonial: multiple coordinated cells with little specialisation or division of labour.
Y is multicellular: distinct specialised cell types are organised into tissues and depend on coordinated functions.
Cell number alone does not separate the categories.
Answer: classify from degree of specialisation and integration ✓
scenes.caption: X: colonial with little division of labour. Y: multicellular with specialised tissues.

voiceover.text: Quick check. Organism X is a small sheet of similar flagellated cells that coordinate movement but show little division of labour. Organism Y contains specialised nerve, muscle and digestive cells organised into tissues. X is colonial because its cells remain similar and division of labour is limited. Y is multicellular because specialised cell types are organised into tissues and integrated functions. Cell number by itself is not enough, and neither is a universal claim about whether an isolated cell can survive.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Unicellular: one generalist cell performs every function of life (Amoeba, Paramecium).
Colonial: near-identical cells live together, with little specialisation, each largely independent (Volvox).
Multicellular: specialised cells that depend on each other; none survives alone.
Moving up the levels, specialisation rises and independence falls.
Classify by specialisation and interdependence, never by cell number.
scenes.finalPrompt: Classifying an organism? Ask: specialised cells, and could one live alone?
scenes.caption: Unicellular, colonial, multicellular: specialisation up, independence down.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. A unicellular organism is one generalist cell that performs every function of life. A colonial organism is near-identical cells living together, with little specialisation, and each cell is largely independent. A multicellular organism is specialised cells that depend on each other, so none can survive alone. As you move up the levels, specialisation rises and independence falls. And classify by specialisation and interdependence, never by the number of cells. Next lesson, we'll see why cells can't just keep getting bigger.
